title: Zero trust inside the cluster
scenario: "If one pod in the cluster is compromised, can it call our customer API directly? Show me, don't tell me." — Security architect
mission: Prove the portal pods only accept traffic from the ingress controller, the metric collectors and the smoke test, using Cilium-enforced NetworkPolicies.
objectives: Read a NetworkPolicy and predict allowed flows
Test a denied flow with a throwaway pod
Explain why the network policy engine matters

steps.title: Read the policy
steps.detail: Which namespaces and pods may reach port 8080?

steps.title: Check the engine
steps.detail: A NetworkPolicy without an enforcing engine is just YAML.
steps.command: az aks show -g rg-mfs-portal-lab -n aks-mfs-portal-lab --query networkProfile.networkPolicy

steps.title: Test from outside
steps.detail: Run a disposable curl pod in the default namespace and call the API service. Expect a timeout. Delete the pod afterwards.

criteria.text: The allow-ingress NetworkPolicy exists in portal-dev and portal-prod
The cluster network policy engine is cilium
No debug pods are left in the default namespace

expectedResult: Lateral movement to the API is blocked and you can demonstrate it.

concepts.title: Default allow and how to flip it
concepts.body: Without NetworkPolicies every pod can talk to every pod. As soon as a pod is *selected* by an ingress NetworkPolicy, it only accepts the traffic that some policy explicitly allows — everything else is dropped.

concepts.title: Selectors
concepts.body: `podSelector` chooses the pods the policy protects; `from` lists allowed sources by `namespaceSelector` and/or `podSelector`. The label `kubernetes.io/metadata.name` exists on every namespace and is handy for selecting namespaces by name.

concepts.title: An engine must enforce it
concepts.body: A NetworkPolicy is just YAML unless the network dataplane enforces it. This cluster uses Cilium (`network_policy = "cilium"`).

example.title: testing a flow with a throwaway pod
example.body: Run a temporary pod in another namespace and try to reach a service; `--rm` deletes it on exit. A timeout means the policy blocked it:
example.code: kubectl run nettest --rm -it --restart=Never -n default --image=curlimages/curl -- curl -m 5 http://<svc>.<ns>

glossary.def: Traffic between workloads inside the cluster.
Rules for incoming / outgoing pod traffic.

recovery: If the ingress returns 502 after a policy change, the ingress namespace was not allowed — revert the PR.
dont: Do not disable the policy to debug
Do not leave debug pods running
hints: A pod selected by any ingress policy denies everything not explicitly allowed.

interview.question: How do you limit east-west traffic in Kubernetes, and how do you prove it works?
followUps: What does Cilium add over basic NetworkPolicy?

debrief: Selecting the pods with an ingress policy flips them to default-deny for ingress; only listed sources pass. Enforcement depends on the dataplane (Cilium here). Egress policies are the next step to stop data exfiltration.

checker.plan: Read-only: kubectl get networkpolicy -A -o json, az aks show networkProfile, kubectl get pods -n default.
